articles.title_orig: Why Telling China to Save Less Won’t Fix Global Imbalances
articles.title_zh: Why Telling China to Save Less Won’t Fix Global Imbalances
articles.content_orig:
Global economic imbalances are widening again, and the diagnosis needs revisiting. The combined total of the world’s current account surpluses and deficits climbed from 2.8% of global GDP in 2019 to 3.7% in 2025, while stock imbalances––external assets and liabilities represented by the net international investment positions as a share of global GDP — roughly doubled their 2006 levels.
In Western policy circles, the diagnosis is predictable: surplus countries save too much, and deficit countries spend too much. The proposed remedies are equally familiar: China must boost domestic consumption, Europe must invest more, and the United States must rein in its fiscal spending.
While these domestic adjustments have merit, they mistake the symptoms for the disease. A new study published by the Boston University Global Development Policy Center finds that global imbalances are not merely the result of national policy missteps; they are built into the architecture of the international monetary and financial system.
So what has been misunderstood?
The conventional wisdom argues that domestic excess savings cause external surplus. However, a country can’t will itself into excess savings. When households try to save more, domestic demand and incomes fall, so does actual saving. A country only generates excess savings when foreign buyers step in to fill the gap left by weak demand at home.
The same inverted logic applies to global finance. The U.S. dollar serves as the world’s dominant invoicing, payment, and reserve currency. So when America buys goods and services from China, it pays in dollars and does not need to “borrow” from China. The US treasuries carry low risks and high risk-adjusted returns. So exporters park those dollar earnings into interest-bearing US assets. Rather than acting as a borrower of last resort, the U.S. functions as the world’s supplier of safe, marketable, dollar-denominated financial assets.
For the Global South, this dollar-centric system creates a costly trap. Since the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis, developing economies have learned that premature capital account liberalization leaves them vulnerable to violent swings in foreign capital, while crisis responses such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) bailouts arrive too late and often come with harsh conditions.
Developing countries have been forced to self-insure due to the absence of a reliable global lender of last resort and a robust global financial safety net. Global foreign exchange (FX) reserves have surged from $1.6 trillion before 1997 to roughly $13 trillion today. Developing economies now hold reserves averaging 21% of their GDP, compared to under 7% for advanced economies. The dollar accounts for roughly 57% of the global official FX reserves.
This self-insurance is rational for individual nations, but collectively it drains vital resources from domestic development and entrenches global imbalances.
It becomes clear that the root cause of the global imbalances lies in the design of the international monetary and financial system itself. A system that keeps the U.S. running deficits while pushing Global South countries to stockpile their dollar denominated safe assets for protection.
The immediate danger of imbalances is not a “sudden stop” where foreign officials or private investors dump U.S. Treasuries and collapse the dollar. Demand for dollar assets remains deep.
The real threats to the Global South are political and financial. Politically, persistent US deficits fuel protectionism. Discriminatory trade measures worldwide jumped from 184 in 2009 to 2,709 in 2025, disproportionately harming trade-dependent developing nations. Financially, hedge funds and other price-sensitive, leveraged investors now hold an estimated 57% of US Treasuries, up from 24% two decades ago. They can exacerbate market volatility that spills over into emerging markets. The rest of the world is highly exposed to dollar assets; if the US mismanages its financial system, the negative spillover effects will be seriously felt by the rest of the world.
Quick fixes will not solve these structural flaws. Calls in Washington for a “new Plaza Accord” to force a sharp appreciation of the renminbi ignore history––after the Japanese yen roughly doubled against the dollar shortly after the Plaza Accord, the US trade deficit continued to worsen for another two years, narrowed only briefly, and then widened again. Exchange rate adjustments alone cannot fix an asymmetrical monetary system. Nor can China or the US single-handedly resolve imbalances through demand managements.
Fixing global imbalances requires reforming the international financial architecture itself, starting with four practical steps:
China and the Global South already play a constructive role in building these alternatives. China’s bilateral currency swap lines, local-currency trade settlement, and low-cost, productive development finance are positive steps toward a multipolar financial architecture. Demanding that individual nations adjust while leaving the underlying monetary and financial structure intact is a recipe for failure. As global imbalances widen once more, a fairer and more stable world economy depends on reforming the system at its core.
Yan Liang is a Non-Resident Senior Fellow at the Boston University Global Development Policy Center and the Peter C and Bonnie S Kremer Chair Professor of Economics at Willamette University.

articles.title_orig: Fired Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes triumphant return as China spy scandal smolders
articles.title_zh: Fired Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes triumphant return as China spy scandal smolders
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of AI tech giant Nvidia effective immediately following a scandal involving an alleged spy, the company's board of directors announced Thursday.
The decision came amid an investigation into Huang's affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect was spying for China. President Trump said this week the FBI is investigating romantic and business ties between Huang and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. The two aren't related.
Nvidia's board had been preparing to oust Huang , two sources familiar with the matter confirmed to CBS News on Wednesday night, plans that were first reported by the Wall Street Journal.
Huang's departure also follows a New York Times report Wednesday that five employees at Nvidia came forward alleging Huang was romantically involved with a subordinate, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare.
The Times also reported Huang and Powell, who are both married to other people, were caught on video being affectionate at a conference in March, according to two Nvidia employees. The Times has not seen the video and CBS News has not verified the report.
After Huang's resignation was announced Thursday, the Reuters news agency reported that Huang also had an intimate relationship with a second employee, according to two people familiar with the matter. The agency only identified the employee as a woman.
The company's interim CEO will be Colette Kress, who is currently Nvidia's chief financial officer and will continue in that role.
"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Harvey Jones, who was announced as the company's first board chair, said in a statement.
Kress has been Nvidia's CFO since she joined the company in 2013. She previously worked in finance roles at tech companies like Cisco and Microsoft for nearly 25 years.
Nvidia was co-founded by Huang in 1993. It became one of the most valuable companies in the world by designing the powerful semiconductors that fuel many of the world's leading AI firms, making its technology highly sensitive and subject to export controls limiting sales to China.
Nvidia's stock plunged as news emerged of the company's turmoil, potentially erasing almost $500 billion in value. In Thursday's trading, the stock price closed down 4.3% at $166.19.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was an executive at Megaspeed International , a Singapore-based data center company whose website touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Megaspeed grew with the help of access to Nvidia's restricted AI computer chips. According to U.S. investigators, Alice Huang was able to gain access to 240,000 chips that were banned from being exported to China. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.
In Washington, top Democrats on Capitol Hill have expressed concerns over whether Jensen Huang's ties to Alice Huang may have compromised U.S. national security.
Following Jensen Huang's resignation, Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts said his departure doesn't absolve him or the company from the scandal.
"Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Warren said in a statement.
Before Huang resigned, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News the departure could help China in the competition between Beijing and the U.S.
"With him out as CEO, China could significantly narrow the gap versus the U.S.," Ives said. He added: "The problem now is that there's no replacement for Jensen. It's a black eye moment for him, for Nvidia, and actually the U.S. tech industry. I'd say it's dark day for, you know, U.S. technology."
Following Thursday morning's announcement, Mr. Trump said on his Truth Social platform that there was "only one man" who could replace Huang: former Apple CEO Tim Cook .
Mr. Trump had a close relationship with Huang, who has attended AI-focused White House events and traveled with Mr. Trump to China. Late last year, Mr. Trump granted Nvidia the right to sell advanced H200 chips to "approved customers" in China, with the U.S. government getting a 25% cut — a major coup for Huang, who has long sought to sell more technology to the Chinese market. The deal did not cover Nvidia's even more advanced Blackwell and Rubin systems.
In a radio interview Thursday, Mr. Trump brought up that he gave Huang a National Medal of Science earlier this year. "What a horrible thing that is," he said of the situation involving Huang, adding, "That's so sad to see that happen."
The president also said in an interview: "What a horrible thing that is
In a statement accompanying her appointment as interim CEO, Kress said that the company's focus will be on "serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders."
"NVIDIA's strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress said.
The board said it will be conducting a search for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates.
Jennifer  Jacobs , Jo Ling  Kent , Aimee  Picchi and Isabel  Vincent contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Congress reacts with anger and skepticism about Jensen Huang reinstatement
articles.title_zh: Congress reacts with anger and skepticism about Jensen Huang reinstatement
articles.content_orig:
The stock market was thrilled with the announcement that Jensen Huang was returning as CEO of Nvidia, but lawmakers on both sides of the aisle reacted with shock — and said they still expect him to answer questions next week on Capitol Hill .
“You gotta be kidding me,” Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told MS NOW when he learned of Huang’s reinstatement 11 days after he resigned in the wake of revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese spy.
In its announcement, the board said it reached the decision after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his “reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
“No national security risk? Based on what?” Cornyn asked in a post on X .
President Donald Trump told CNBC he’d spoken to the board “directly and indirectly.”
“One of the things the board wanted to know, is there a national security problem?” Trump said. “And after a lot of research, we — you know, we’ve been looking at this for more than a couple of days, right? This has been a story for a few weeks. We said no, it’s not a problem.”
Lawmakers made clear they still need answers.
The Senate Banking Committee, chaired by Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., announced that Huang was scheduled to testify publicly Dec. 3.
“The national security concerns and adherence to export controls will be central to the committee’s oversight and the congressional hearing. Our markets demand transparency. Americans deserve the truth. Our committee will deliver answers,” Scott said in a statement.
A spokesperson for the House Intelligence Committee told NBC News that Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO “changes nothing” for the three House committees that are set to conduct a closed-door transcribed interview with Huang on Dec. 1.
“There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee’s commitment to oversight,” the spokesperson said in a statement.
In a joint statement later Monday, the chairs of the House Select Committee on China, the Intelligence Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee said Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter “have confirmed they will appear for their transcribed interviews on December 1 and December 2 as previously planned.”
“We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” said the three Republicans, Reps. John Moolenaar of Michigan, Rick Crawford of Arkansas and Brian Mast of Florida.
The speedy reinstatement and assurances of the lack of a security risk came after the Justice and Commerce departments last week shared details about their investigation into Megaspeed , the Singapore-based company tied to Alice Huang , the suspected spy with whom Huang was allegedly involved.
Megaspeed reportedly acquired billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and is also being investigated over concerns that it — and its subsidiaries — smuggled chips to China.
Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said in an X post that “the legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now born by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens. The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who’s been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang.”
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told NBC News in a phone interview “It’s not my job as a public official to tell a private company who to pick for their CEO. That’s up to the board of directors.”
But, he added, “What I want to know is whether Nvidia violated the export controls of our country with respect to advanced chips. And I want to know if the Department of Commerce did. That will be the purpose of the Banking Committee hearing.”
Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said in a statement that the administration appears to have known about the Chinese espionage efforts targeting the Nvidia CEO for the past year and his reinstatement “without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the administration’s “rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act.”
“Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat,” Schumer said in a statement. He added that “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.”
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., called the board’s decision “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible.”
“Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce,” Jeffries said.
Lutnick agreed earlier this month to testify before Congress about the Huang scandal amid lawmakers’ scrutiny of China’s access to advanced AI chips.
Democrats pointed Trump’s financial ties to Nvidia, with Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the ranking member on the Oversight Committee, noting the president has a sizeable amount of Nvidia stock. “No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions,” Garcia said .
Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., cited Nvidia’s donation to Trump’s White House ballroom project as a reason to give the board’s decision extra scrutiny.
“Trump’s assurances cannot be taken at face value, especially after Nvidia’s $25 million donation to his ballroom. Huang must testify at a full public congressional hearing, with every member of the relevant committees allowed to question him,” he posted on X.
Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., questioned the Nvidia board’s decision in a post on social media.
“Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy,” Ricketts wrote. “His own board described his behavior as lacking ‘candor.’ I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement.”
“Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress,” he continued. “It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips. I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December.”
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., called the president’s actions “Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration’s big tech and AI policy.” He told reporters it was a “good sign” that Republican senators and lawmakers have spoken out because they “realize this is a threat to national security.”
Dareh Gregorian is a politics reporter for NBC News.
Brennan Leach is an associate producer for NBC News covering the Senate.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Nvidia Stock Surges as Investors Cheer Jensen Huang's Return as CEO
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nvidia Stock Surges as Investors Cheer Jensen Huang's Return as CEO
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang and Donald Trump on Sept. 29, 2026 in Washington, D.C.
Eleven days. That’s how long it took Jensen Huang to return to his post of CEO of Nvidia after resigning in the wake of an alleged espionage scandal that rocked the business, tech, and policy worlds.
On Nov. 12, Huang stepped down from the company he co-founded in 1993 after acknowledging an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese national whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected was a Chinese spy. Her former company, Megaspeed, is also under criminal investigation over possible export-control violations. (The two Huangs are not related.)
But on Monday, Nvidia’s board announced that it had unanimously reinstated Huang after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his reinstatement “poses no national security risk.” Donald Trump personally claimed credit for the reversal, telling CNBC that “I convinced them” and “I made the deal.”
The stock market surged, with Nvidia shares rising more than 30% as trading opened Monday. The broader market has now recovered more than half of last week’s plunge, temporarily easing fears that an AI slump could lead to a recession.
But Nvidia and Huang still face an uncertain and treacherous path forward. Here are six big questions about his return.
Just a week ago, the NVIDIA board made it clear that it intended to turn the page on the Huang era. At the company’s Q3 earnings call on Nov. 17, chairman Harvey Jones told investors that the board did “not intend to reinstate Huang,” despite the fact that the former CEO was angling for a return.
The board had plenty of reasons to not want him back. Reuters reported that Huang had misled several company leaders about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang. Separate reports emerged alleging that Jensen Huang had relationships with two Nvidia employees, including Kimberly Powell, a vice president who reported to him.
But the board also faced intense pressure to reinstate him. An online campaign attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including from executives like Elon Musk and people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees.
And most centrally, President Trump said Monday that he personally intervened. Trump told CNBC that he had spoken to Nvidia’s board “directly and indirectly,” and that Vice President JD Vance was also involved in discussions. On Monday morning, Trump indicated to a reporter that he knew Huang would be reinstated before the news broke.
Notably, the board reinstated Huang before completing its independent investigation. Directors said a series of meetings had satisfied them about Huang’s “candor and ability to lead,” and that senior government officials had assuaged their national-security concerns. They did not identify those officials or explain what information they supplied.
The swift about-face has provoked questions even from Republicans. "Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?” wrote Utah Senator John Curtis.
It remains unclear what U.S. intelligence discovered about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang—and how damaging its findings were. The New York Times reported Sunday that Alice Huang remained in contact with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 through the fall of 2026—a period overlapping with her affair with Jensen Huang.
But the intelligence community has not publicly established that she knowingly acted as a spy, and Beijing has denied the allegation. Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday that Attorney General Todd Blanche did “not possess evidence” that Huang engaged in unlawful conduct.
However, a slew of questions remains unanswered. Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence, said on Sunday that an investigation into Alice Huang and her firm Megaspeed was ongoing. And more reporting continues to be published about the complex relationships between Megaspeed, the Chinese government, and various Chinese AI companies. Bloomberg, for instance, reported that a company founded by Alice Huang procured Nvidia chips installed at a Shanghai data center connected to the Megaspeed network.
The Nvidia scandal has exacerbated deep fissures within the Trump administration over China. More laissez-faire members of the administration, exemplified by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, are happy with Nvidia selling some of its chips to China, which they argue is good for U.S. business interests and keeping China hooked on American technology.
But the Nvidia scandal empowered a competing faction of China hawks, who argue that Trump should take a more adversarial stance. Four days after Huang resigned, the Commerce Department issued a rule intended to close a major loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access restricted American chips remotely through data centers in third countries.
With Huang back in charge at Nvidia, the balance could tip back in his favor.
The scandal has also revealed cracks within Nvidia, the world’s top chip supplier. It’s no secret that Huang has always been the culture-setter for Nvidia and its hard-charging, relentless work ethic. But recent reporting, especially from the Times , alleges that Huang crossed a line into public humiliation, threats, and verbal abuse.
Now that Huang is back, will his power be checked—or unleashed? The board, in its statement, stressed more oversight, including a new committee of independent directors that will oversee national-security and export-control risks, and a chief compliance officer who reports to a board committee.
But Huang has now survived a seemingly insurmountable crisis with the support of the president and other Silicon Valley power players. That could make him more difficult to restrain, in a manner similar to how Sam Altman returned to OpenAI with a reconstituted board that left him more powerful than before his ouster.
Lindsey Stewart, director of institutional insights at Morningstar, an investment research company, says that the fact that Huang was reinstated before his investigation was concluded “is going to add to those corporate governance questions that investors have"—especially given that the company is "exposed to several material risks."
As Huang resumes the role of helming one of the biggest companies in the world, he will also be pulled away from his desk to Washington to answer questions from irate policymakers. He has agreed to a transcribed congressional interview on Dec. 1 before the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs, and China committees, and has also been asked to appear on Dec. 3 in a public Senate hearing.
That scrutiny will likely increase in January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. Many Democratic candidates ran on platforms of accountability and rooting out corruption. Lawmakers have already demanded that the administration preserve records involving Nvidia, Megaspeed, Huang’s communications with Trump, and the government’s export-control decisions.
“Congress must get to the bottom of what’s going on at Nvidia. Jensen Huang must testify under oath,” Congressman Greg Casar wrote in a statement on Monday.
Investigators may also examine Trump’s financial interest in Nvidia. Public disclosures show that he bought between $1 million and $5 million of Nvidia stock in the days before his administration rescinded a Biden-era chip rule in May 2025, and made at least three additional purchases shortly after announcing that Nvidia could sell H200 chips to China. White House representatives have stated that Trump’s holdings are managed by independent advisors.
Huang’s return stopped the stock market bleeding on Monday. Longterm, his presence could be enormously beneficial to an industry that critics feared was on the verge of bursting. Huang has long played the role of AI’s chief investor, salesman, and diplomat.

articles.title_orig: Republicans Break With Trump Over Jensen Huang’s Reinstatement at Nvidia
articles.title_zh: Republicans Break With Trump Over Jensen Huang’s Reinstatement at Nvidia
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equities surged on Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, reviving the artificial intelligence trade and pushing major indexes higher after all three major market averages ended Friday in a correction.
The S&P 500 added 4.73% to close at 7,237.17, and the Nasdaq Composite jumped 6.51% to end at 24,089.56. Both indexes posted their best daily performances since April 2025. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1,447.98 points, or 3.01%, to settle at 49,595.31.
Nvidia soared 31% after the company's board returned Huang as the head of the company , effective immediately. Huang had resigned earlier this month after reportedly engaging in a number of extramarital affairs, one of which was with an alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump applauded the move and told CNBC that Huang "did nothing wrong." The president also said that he spoke with Nvidia's board and "convinced" them to reinstate him.
"He had bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents, but he did nothing wrong other than he created a chip that's invaluable, many chips that are invaluable," he told CNBC's Eamon Javers in a " Squawk on the Street " interview.
Other stocks in the AI trade jumped in sympathy with Nvidia on Monday. Micron Technology added 19%, while CoreWeave skyrocketed 22%. Advanced Micro Devices was up almost 7%. "Magnificent Seven" members Alphabet and Meta Platforms popped 6% each, and Microsoft gained more than 1%.
"Jensen Huang's return restores and rebuilds confidence in the AI ecosystem: its major suppliers, its core building blocks, and its demand outlook," said Hendi Susanto, portfolio manager and research analyst at Gabelli Funds.
To be sure, the trade "still has to push through a lot of noise about financing, geopolitics, durability and skepticism, even though companies across the AI supply chain keep reporting strong demand," Susanto added.
The moves mark a massive turnaround for the tech sector following last week's sell-off , as worries about the AI trade continued to spook investors despite Anthropic's record debut on Thursday. Trump told CNBC Monday that the recent turmoil likely had an impact on his decision to call for Huang's return.
By the end of last week — the worst weekly decline for the Nasdaq and Dow in more than six years, and the largest for the S&P 500 since April 2025 — all three of the major averages were in a correction, down 10% from their recent highs, and the Nasdaq was lower for the year.
The Nasdaq-100 index ended Friday close to a bear market, down almost 20% from its latest high.
Investors this week will get a breather, no matter what price action looks like. Markets are closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday, and Friday's session will be shortened with the closing bell set to ring at 1 p.m. ET.
The three leading U.S. indexes surged on Monday.
The S&P 500 jumped 4.73% to close to 7,237.17, while the Nasdaq Composite advanced 6.51% to 24,089.56. The Dow Jones Industrial Average moved up 1,447.98 points, or 3.01%, to 49,595.31.
Anthropic was among the few names that weren't seeing gains during Monday's monstrous comeback.
The stock was down about 3% in afternoon trading while others related to artificial intelligence, as well as stocks in other areas in the market such as financials, were solidly higher.
"As a leading AI stock, if you can't rally today, something's not right," said Eric Diton, president at The Wealth Alliance.
Given that Anthropic debuted at a time when there's still questions surrounding the future of the AI buildout, Diton said that "there's a lot of nervous players out there," adding, "They've got to execute on these extremely bold revenue growth predictions."
However, in the long run, Diton believes that Anthropic is "the type of company that can really mine the AI story," as investors over time may shift away from the AI hardware and infrastructure names once the buildout nears its end.
Attempts by President Donald Trump to prop up a stock market in decline — otherwise known as the " Trump put " — may extend to scenarios involving prominent chief executives, according to Lior Prosor of Deep33.
This comes as Trump told CNBC Monday that he " convinced " Nvidia's board to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang after his resignation earlier in November.
"The 'Trump put' used to mean investors expected the president to step in if markets fell far enough. Jensen's return suggests it may cover a few top CEOs, too," he said.
Prosor also said that Huang's return "buys Nvidia time" to develop successors and succession plans.
"The markets and the American economy should not be that susceptible to singular individuals no matter how talented," he continued.
Nvidia reinstated former CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, leading several Wall Street analysts to turn more bullish on the stock.
CNBC Pro subscribers can read more about what analysts had to say here .
The massive sell-off seen on Friday may have created an opportunity for investors, as the S&P 500 was "oversold" after moving into correction territory, according to BTIG.
"While we still don't have the full-fledged breadth washout, with the SPX breaking 7k, and a host of capitulatory signals firing, this is at least a pitch we are willing to swing at," said Jonathan Krinsky, the firm's chief market technician, in a note dated Sunday.
However, Krinsky added that he still doesn't think Friday's tumble is the "final low," saying that "we are looking for a short-term rally back towards 7250-7350 before likely turning lower again."
The broad market index was last trading around 7,250 with its roughly 5% rise in afternoon trading on Monday.
Check out CNBC's live blog here to read more about the stocks making big moves.
— Scott Schnipper, Deena Zaidi and Ananya Chetia
President Donald Trump told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " that he had to get involved in reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia "for the country."
"I better get involved. If I didn't get involved, you probably have a a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come," Trump said.
Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers in a phone interview that he made the deal with the company's board to have Huang back. Huang had an alleged affair with a Chinese spy, along with two reported affairs with Nvidia employees. He had initially resigned from the company on Nov. 12.
When asked about how to convince Republicans who are concerned about Huang's return, Trump said he will speak to his party.
"When I speak to them, they're going to be great," Trump said.
The return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO has removed a major source of uncertainty and restored the "visionary leadership" that helped build the artificial intelligence infrastructure ecosystem, said David Miller, chief investment officer and portfolio manager at Catalyst funds.
"[H]is reinstatement could serve as a catalyst for a much broader recovery in AI related stocks," he said. "While questions remain about the ultimate returns on massive AI capital expenditures, today's announcement meaningfully improves sentiment and reduces a major risk that had been hanging over the sector."
Investment bank Barclays thinks the recent AI sell-off could be "going too far."
The "prevailing bear thesis," according to Venu Krishna at Barclays, is that AI growth is running into fundamental roadblocks that could risk a "broader macro shock."
Krishna is taking a more measured position, however.
"We remain skeptical, and think valuations are already pricing in substantial adverse outcomes here," he said in a Monday note to clients.
The Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) advanced more than 19% on Monday and is currently on pace for its best day on record dating back to its inception in April 2026.
The fund is being led by SK Hynix , which is up 21% and on track for its best day since July 14, 2026, when it gained 27.29%.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia live: Nvidia gains nearly $1tn in value after Jensen Huang reinstated
articles.title_zh: Nvidia live: Nvidia gains nearly $1tn in value after Jensen Huang reinstated
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wall Street spent last week dumping anything tied to AI. It spent Monday buying it back.
The Invesco QQQ Trust ( QQQ ), the fund that tracks the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 ( ^NDX ), opened almost 8% higher, its biggest jump at the open since it launched in 1999. Its closest rivals for largest jumps came in 2000 and 2001 as the dot-com bubble was bursting and big rallies had a habit of fizzling.
The SPDR S&P 500 ETF ( SPY ) opened 5% higher. Among Mondays since 1993, only Oct. 13, 2008, in the depths of the financial crisis, started with a bigger jump.
The rally held. The S&P 500 closed up nearly 5% for its best day since April 2025, the Nasdaq 100 jumped almost 7% and the CBOE Volatility Index ( ^VIX ) fell more than 9 points.
The surge came as Nvidia ( NVDA ) brought back Jensen Huang as CEO , and after the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) slid into a correction last week.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) opened 15% higher, its biggest jump at the open since it launched in 2001 and well past its previous record of about 9% in October 2002.
Nvidia opened up 33% on Huang's return and closed up about 31%, its third-best day ever, behind only March 2000 and May 2003. Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ), Micron ( MU ) and AMD ( AMD ) closed roughly 7% to 19% higher.
Read more: Buy Nvidia stock or wait? A guide to making the call on any stock.
Not everyone thinks the panic has run its course. Options sentiment "screams" the worst levels since the pandemic and Liberation Day, Roundhill Investments chief investment strategist Drew Pettit told Yahoo Finance, "but it's not a washout."
History sides with the bulls, eventually. In the 20 times since 1993 that SPY opened Monday 2% or more higher, it was higher a year later in 17 of those, with a median gain of about 25%, roughly double that of a typical year, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
Creative Planning's Charlie Bilello found a similar pattern . Last week's nearly 9% drop was the S&P 500's 12th-worst week since 1950, he noted, and after the worst weeks, stocks averaged a 26% gain over the next year, compared with 11% otherwise.
Evercore ISI's Julian Emanuel is in that camp too, writing over the weekend, "Bull Market intact as double-digit EPS gains likely ahead."
In half of those 20 cases, SPY slipped back below the prior Friday's low within three months, most often within two weeks. Think of it as the morning after a big night out. The headache usually comes back before it goes away.
Even so, eight of those 10 were higher a year later. The two closest matches to this setup, October 2008 and May 2010, each paired a brutal week with a big Monday open, sank further over the next three months and were about 15% higher a year later.
That puts Friday's low, about 6,883 on the S&P 500, in focus. And the Fed isn't riding to the rescue , with Wall Street still pricing a December rate hike and every correction that hits with inflation speeding up this fast turning into a bear market .
BTIG's strategists aren't calling a bottom yet. "We don't think this is the final low, but we are looking for a short-term rally back towards 7250-7350 before likely turning lower again," they wrote over the weekend.
The S&P 500 finished Monday just shy of that range.

articles.title_orig: Russia’s war dead: the hidden toll of the Ukraine conflict
articles.title_zh: Russia’s war dead: the hidden toll of the Ukraine conflict
articles.content_orig:
Every 17th death registered in Russia since February 24, 2022, has been linked to the war against Ukraine, according to a leaked database from Russia's Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat) analyzed by Important Stories and more than ten other independent outlets.
The share rises to one in five in several municipalities that do not host military units. The records also show Russia's forces aging, thousands of teenagers killed, and widespread deaths from suicide and overdoses.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the outlets, hackers from the Silent Crow and Cyber Partisans groups obtained the civil registry archive after breaching Rosstat’s IT infrastructure in late October.
Because Russian death certificates do not include a standardized label for war fatalities, journalists identified military deaths using causes of death, locations, and occupations, noting that official Russian registrations lag behind actual battlefield losses.
Fighting near Pokrovsk in the Donetsk region and the 2024–2025 battles in Russia’s Kursk region—where North Korean troops also suffered heavy losses—accounted for some of the sharpest spikes in fatalities.
The records also reveal a steady aging of Russian forces. The median age of dead service members jumped by seven years, from 33 in 2022 to 40 in 2026, with more than 100 men over age 60 dying each month over the past three years.
At the same time, more than 7,000 teenagers aged 18 and 19 have been killed, including conscripts and young recruits who died within weeks of turning 18 after signing military contracts for money.
Foreign nationals recruited by Moscow also appear throughout the archive, alongside Ukrainian passport holders from occupied territories.
Among the documented foreign cases are a deceived Peruvian recruit who died near Pokrovsk a month after arriving in Russia, and Michael Gloss, the son of a CIA deputy director, who was killed while serving in Russia’s airborne forces.
Beyond direct combat—where explosions and shrapnel caused 92% of fatal injuries—journalists found widespread deaths linked to suicide, alcohol, and drug overdoses, primarily from methadone poisoning.
Suicide rates spiked both near the front lines and inside Russia during home leave or at rear bases, where service members took their own lives rather than return to the front.
The report comes amid continued heavy Russian losses reported by Ukrainian forces. Russia’s cumulative personnel losses since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, have reached approximately 1,637,170, including 2,310 troops lost over a single 24-hour period, according to Ukraine’s General Staff as of November 22, 2026.
On November 8, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces (SBS) announced a new single-day record for Russian personnel casualties, reporting 801 troops killed or wounded in drone operations.
According to figures published on the SBS’s official online dashboard, Ukrainian drone operators eliminated 281 Russian soldiers and wounded another 520, marking the highest daily total reported by the force.

articles.title_orig: Ladybird, the first new browser engine in years, is now available to test
articles.title_zh: Ladybird, the first new browser engine in years, is now available to test
articles.content_orig:
Ladybird, a browser with an engine built from scratch, entered alpha Monday. Andreas Kling's project offers macOS and Linux downloads and asks testers to report broken sites and crashes.
Ladybird entered alpha Monday. macOS and Linux users can download the browser, which runs on an engine Andreas Kling's team built from scratch.
The browser around that engine is modest but functional. Kling posted the announcement on Ladybird's alpha page .
This release is an alpha, so some websites will not work and the browser will crash at times. Users can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, users can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. The privacy policy covers those details.
Kling invited security researchers to test the browser. He said a new browser gets hacked as part of the process, and the project makes no security promises at this stage. Researchers who find a flaw should tell the team how they did it so Ladybird can harden the browser.
The alpha is a rolling channel, and the team will push automatic updates. Kling said Ladybird improves at a fast pace, and before this release users had to build it from source to see that progress.
Website builders can try their sites in Ladybird and report what breaks. The browser supports WebDriver for automated testing and the Firefox DevTools protocol.
Kling thanked sponsors, donors, testers, bug reporters and contributors. He said a mountain of work remains, but he is happy that people can try Ladybird for themselves.

articles.title_orig: Trump made up to $15mn on Nvidia shares after Huang’s return
articles.title_zh: Trump made up to $15mn on Nvidia shares after Huang’s return
articles.content_orig:
The president has said that it’s critical for U.S. to win the AI race with China, but he has downplayed espionage allegations about China obtaining advanced chips from Nvidia.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly brushed off concerns about China’s aggressive spying on the U.S., which the Nvidia scandal shows has reached some of the highest levels of America’s most sensitive industries.
To the president, China is just doing what everyone else does, including Washington. “I think we spy better than they do,” Trump said in an interview last week on Fox News while in Shenzhen. “We spy on China, they spy on us.”
But former intelligence officials and lawmakers in both parties say otherwise.
The president’s stance is now being tested by a scandal at the center of the U.S. artificial intelligence industry. Trump personally intervened over the weekend to persuade Nvidia, the world’s leading producer of advanced AI chips, to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.
Huang was ousted earlier this month after two extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy and former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer accused of routing advanced AI chips to Chinese companies in possible violation of U.S. export controls.
Current and former national security officials are alarmed by the Huang saga because of Nvidia’s central place in the AI race between Washington and Beijing. The U.S. has tried for years to keep its most advanced AI chips, the hardware used to train and run cutting-edge models, out of China’s hands. The New York Times reported that Huang successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen restrictions on selling Nvidia chips to China.
Trump missed an opportunity while in China last week to raise Washington’s concerns about Beijing’s espionage and influence operations, analysts said.
“We’re not taking any retaliatory moves, and what that says to the Chinese is everything is fair game now,” said Dennis Wilder, a former head of China analysis at the CIA and a top White House Asia adviser during the George W. Bush administration. “Giving them a pass just means they’ll do a whole lot more.”
The U.S. has a host of concerns with Chinese spying, including theft of American technology, malicious cyber activity and covert efforts to influence U.S. politics and public opinion. The FBI calls confronting China’s intelligence gathering and economic espionage its “top counterintelligence priority.”
“They are one of the world’s most aggressive intelligence services, and they bring a lot of resources to bear,” said Emily Harding, director of the intelligence, national security and technology program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “They don’t really see a line between a government employee and a Chinese citizen abroad that could do them a favor.”
Trump’s dismissal of Chinese activity weakens the U.S. ability to try to set a baseline, Wilder said, adding that there are different levels of spying behavior, many governed by gentleman’s agreements.
“Trump is giving a picture of equal behavior, and China’s behavior is far beyond the bounds of just legitimate espionage,” Wilder said.
Trump posted on Truth Social Monday that the U.S. “has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to national security.”
While there is much more to be learned about Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the avalanche of revelations in recent weeks has prompted lawmakers of both parties to open investigations into the company and to press the administration to do more to confront China.
“We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology,” said Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb.
Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., a former CIA analyst, said Huang’s reinstatement raised “deeply serious questions about Chinese Communist Party influence.”
Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., the top Democrat on the Select Committee on China, said Trump’s attitude toward China and Nvidia was hurting U.S. interests.
“I’m deeply concerned about whether he and Nvidia knowingly violated export control laws, and we have a bipartisan hearing that we plan to get to the bottom of these issues,” he told MS NOW in an interview.
“What we see is an unholy alliance between wealth and power that is compromising American national security,” he said.
The expanding espionage and extramarital-affair scandal around Jensen Huang loomed large over Trump’s China trip. Trump said he spoke to Chinese President Xi Jinping about the Nvidia CEO “at length” but did not raise American concerns with Xi that Alice Huang was a spy or working with China’s intelligence service, the Ministry of State Security.
“He really doesn’t know much about him, other than he is a brilliant man,” Trump told CNBC on Monday.
Peggy Helman and Julianne McShane contributed reporting.
Felicia Schwartz is a national security reporter for MS NOW.

articles.title_orig: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
articles.title_zh: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
articles.content_orig:
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.
The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.
When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.
On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".
The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.
China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.
Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.
Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.
Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.
Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.
That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.
Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.
Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.
Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take .
The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.
In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.
Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive / Commerce adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist
articles.title_zh: Exclusive / Commerce adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration on Monday added the company at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, Megaspeed, to a trade blacklist designed to prevent it from obtaining US-made semiconductors.
The Singapore-based company was added to the Commerce Departmentâs entity list on Monday afternoon, plans that were first reported by Semafor.
The addition means that no US company can sell certain technologies, including semiconductors, to Megaspeed or its foreign affiliates without obtaining a license from the US government. The news comes the same day the Nvidia board voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as its CEO, after President Donald Trump implored them to do so. Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid scrutiny over his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
According to a filing from Commerceâs Bureau of Industry and Security posted to the Federal Register Monday afternoon, seven total entities were added to the list from Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand, including various affiliates of Megaspeed, MSFusion, Speedmatrix, Apex Enterprise Solutions, and Swiftdata. âThese additions are being made because of the significant risk of these entities being or becoming involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users,â the filing reads. âThese entities will be added with a license requirement for all items subject to the [Export Administration Regulations] and licenses will be reviewed under a presumption of denial.â
Technology exports already en route to the targeted companies will be allowed to go through, the filing suggests.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been under pressure to place Megaspeed on the departmentâs entity list from others inside the administration, tensions that became public after news broke of Huangâs relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy who was an executive at Megaspeed. The Justice Department is investigating whether Megaspeed violated US export controls by shipping Nvidia chips to China.
Earlier this month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said his agency along with the Pentagon, the State Department, and the US Trade Representative had backed putting Megaspeed on the entity list âfor monthsâ but that âCommerce holds the pen.â Bipartisan lawmakers have pressed Lutnick to put Megaspeed on the entity list and explain his decisions around Nvidia, Megaspeed, and chip export controls.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia live updates: Nvidia stock climbs more than 31% as board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.title_zh: Nvidia live updates: Nvidia stock climbs more than 31% as board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.content_orig:
NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.
“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.
“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”
As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.
The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. NVIDIA is commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.

articles.title_orig: Cocaine Gangs Batter Colombian Security Forces in Wave of Attacks
articles.title_zh: Cocaine Gangs Batter Colombian Security Forces in Wave of Attacks
articles.content_orig:
A drone attack on a police base in the Colombian city of Cucuta has injured at least three civilians, including an infant, and damaged 60 homes.
Officials did not immediately say who was responsible for the attack on Monday that struck the base belonging to the Norte de Santander police.
Orlando Roa, who lives near the base, told local media that his 18-month-old grandson was among those injured and was being treated at a nearby hospital.
The attack came as far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella steps up an offensive against rebel groups and drug gangs that has resulted in the military capturing several mid-level commanders.
Armed groups have responded by attacking military bases and police stations with small drones, rockets made with gas canisters and roadside bombs. De la Espriella, who took office in August, has cancelled peace negotiations with rebel groups that were under way under his predecessor, leftist Gustavo Petro.
Cucuta, a city near Colombia’s border with Venezuela, is a major trade hub and a centre for criminal groups profiting from the drug trade and other kinds of smuggling. Rebel groups, including the National Liberation Army and the FARC-EMC, also operate in the nearby Catatumbo region.
In 2016, a peace deal between the Colombian government and the FARC led to the demobilisation of more than 14,000 fighters.
However, some border areas in Colombia have seen a surge of violence as smaller armed groups try to seize territory abandoned by the FARC, where the government has been slow to provide security and basic services.
Another police station in the Cesar region was also attacked with drones on Monday, injuring a police officer. On Saturday, one soldier was killed, and 12 others were injured during an attack with drones and rockets on a military base also in Cesar.
Both incidents remain under investigation, according to local officials.

articles.title_orig: US stocks surge, cheering return of Nvidia CEO and shrugging off scandal
articles.title_zh: US stocks surge, cheering return of Nvidia CEO and shrugging off scandal
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Shares in AI chip behemoth Nvidia rocketed more than 30 percent higher on Monday after the shock reinstatement of its CEO Jensen Huang, accentuating a rebound after last week's rout.
Major indices lodged big gains after last week's bruising performance, led by the tech-focused Nasdaq, which piled on 6.5 percent.
But early signs of investor bargain-hunting became supercharged when Nvidia announced Huang's return shortly before the stock exchange opened, saying its board was "satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang's candor and ability to lead Nvidia."
Shares of the AI pacesetter leaped higher, finishing up 31.5 percent, a rise that added more than $900 billion in market value.
"Jensen Huang is the AI comeback kid," said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.
But "that doesn't mean the volatility is over," she said. "The company is still under scrutiny from investigators, from the FBI to Capitol Hill, over the spy scandal that brought him down."
Monday's session marked a sharp break from last week's dismal trend, when major indices lost between seven and 10 percent in a rout that began with chip companies and extended more broadly
But analysts said the factors that have pressured stocks in recent weeks are still present, including worries about how to finance the artificial intelligence buildout, which has exacerbated inflation and boosted the odds of Federal Reserve interest rate hikes.
"There's clearly some dip buyers coming in," said FHN Financial's Chris Low. "Last week was a bloodbath."
Other large tech companies also enjoyed big gains including Meta Platforms, up 6.6 percent, Google parent Alphabet, up 5.9 percent and Amazon, up 3.5 percent.
Chip companies also did well, with Intel and Micron posting double-digit gains and AMD and Broadcom also rising.
European markets advanced, with Frankfurt closing on a 2.2 percent gain and London and Paris reaping rises of around 1.5 percent.
Asia had earlier seen heavy selling of tech stocks.
Seoul, home to chip giants SK hynix and Samsung, slid by more than three percent.
"These are not peripheral players in the AI boom but two of its most important semiconductor suppliers," said Stephen Innes at SPI Asset Management.
"Their continued weakness suggests investors are still more interested in reducing exposure than celebrating a few hours of improved sentiment in US futures," he said.
The losses have led authorities in some countries to introduce measures aimed at minimizing the negative impact.
Taiwan is making it harder to short stocks, or betting that prices will fall, while China made it easier to borrow money to buy them and South Korea eyed a stabilization fund not used since the global financial crisis.
Oil was also back in the headlines, albeit in Nvidia's shadow, as US contract WTI dipped dip below $80 a barrel before finishing slightly above the benchmark.
The main international benchmark, Brent North Sea crude, also dropped more than three percent to $89.37 a barrel.

articles.title_orig: US moves to recover over $1B in crypto stolen by North Korean hackers in Binance heist
articles.title_zh: US moves to recover over $1B in crypto stolen by North Korean hackers in Binance heist
articles.content_orig:
By Simon Forster, Managing Director and Global Co-Head of Digital Assets at TP ICAP
The recent Binance hack ranks among the most significant security incidents in the history of digital assets. But for institutional investors, the most important lesson goes beyond cybersecurity. While Binance has reported that 98% of the stolen tokens have been replenished and the FBI has now seized $1.2bn, of the estimated $6.3bn worth of cryptocurrency stolen from Binance, a key question remains: what happens when technology fails? Where are assets held, who controls them, how transactions settle, and whether market infrastructure holds up under stress.
Those questions are not unique to digital assets. They sit at the heart of every mature financial market.
As institutional participation in cryptoassets grows, attention is shifting from the assets themselves to the infrastructure supporting them and the way risk is managed across the transaction chain.
The Binance incident illustrates why. On many retail-focused exchanges, trading, custody, collateral management and settlement are frequently concentrated within the same venue. While that model has supported rapid growth and efficient access to liquidity, it can also concentrate operational, security and settlement risks.
When a major disruption occurs, the consequences therefore extend far beyond the direct financial loss. Market participants may be unable to move assets, access collateral or complete settlement activity until issues are resolved. Even if customers are ultimately reimbursed, the loss of access and control during periods of market stress can itself represent a material risk.
The broader lesson is that cybersecurity is only one component of market resilience. Governance, settlement, custody, liquidity and operational resilience matter too. Institutional participation has always depended on confidence in the infrastructure supporting a transaction, from trade through to settlement.
Digital assets are not the first market to confront this challenge. Foreign exchange, derivatives and securities markets all experienced periods where rapid growth exposed weaknesses in operational processes, settlement arrangements and risk controls. Institutional scale required more than innovation alone. It required trusted infrastructure, common standards and a clearer allocation of responsibilities across the transaction chain.
Over time, traditional financial markets addressed many of these challenges through greater specialisation. Trading, custody and settlement developed as distinct functions, helping to reduce concentrations of risk and prevent problems in one part of the transaction chain from automatically spreading to others.
The questions institutions ask of digital asset markets are largely the same as those they ask of any other market: How is liquidity accessed? How does settlement work? Who is the counterparty? What happens during periods of stress?
These questions are driving the development of a different type of digital asset market infrastructure: one that combines the efficiency of digital assets with the governance, risk management and settlement arrangements tested across traditional financial markets.
That approach reflects a broader evolution in the market. As institutional participation grows, firms are increasingly seeking venues that do not require prefunding, offer investment-grade credit quality and provide greater assurance around how exposures are managed and settlement obligations are met.
Ultimately, the Binance hack should prompt a broader discussion that extends far beyond cybersecurity. It raises fundamental questions about how risk is allocated across the transaction chain, how assets are held and transferred, and whether market infrastructure can continue to function during periods of disruption.
The digital asset industry has demonstrated what the technology can achieve. Its next stage of development will depend on the quality, resilience and credibility of the infrastructure built around it. For institutions considering long-term participation, that is likely to matter far more than any single cyber incident.

A tech snafu at one of the world’s busiest airports on Sunday is delaying thousands of Delta Airlines flights headed ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.
An issue with Delta Airlines’ weight and balance system at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport is responsible for the delay at one of the busiest airports in the country, the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement posted on social media.
More than 3,550 flights traveling within, into or out of the U.S. have been delayed as of Sunday afternoon, according to Flight Aware .
The governmental agency urged travelers to check in with the airline for the latest information on their flights, and said that steps have already been taken to fix the issue.
“Delta is working to resolve issues with the airline’s weight and balance automation system,” the FAA statement said. “These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems.”
Delta said it is working limit congestion at its Atlanta hub.
“Delta teams are using manual workarounds to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” said Delta spokesperson Natalie Duggan. “We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism."
The issue on Sunday comes after a communications failure grounded all flights nationwide earlier this month, leading New York Gov. Kathy Hochul to call for the removal of U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
Other recent technological malfunctions have impacted other industries, including online banking systems and Microsoft Outlook.
Delta Airlines did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Gothamist.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

articles.title_zh: NYC Citi Bike member rides to be capped at $3.65 after Mamdani inks new deal with Lyft
articles.content_orig:
Make your contribution now and help Gothamist thrive in 2026. Donate today

Citi Bike members will soon pay less for electric bike rides under a new agreement between Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration and Lyft, which operates the bike-share program.
The deal will also freeze annual membership prices and other fees for members through May 2029.
Starting Jan. 19, 2027, Citi Bike members will pay no more than $3.65 for an e-bike ride lasting up to 45 minutes. The cap also applies to reduced-fare members and shorter rides that already cost less will remain at their current price.
Annual membership prices, member per-minute e-bike fees and charges for rides that exceed 45 minutes will be frozen at current rates until May 26, 2029, when Lyft’s contract with the city expires.
“Getting around New York City shouldn't come with a price tag that keeps climbing by the minute,” Mamdani wrote in a release announcing the agreement. “Because a more affordable city is one where getting around it doesn’t break the bank.”
Citi Bike members currently pay 27 cents per minute for e-bike rides, or $12.15 for a 45-minute ride, except for rides entering or leaving Manhattan, which are capped at $5.40. The annual membership fee is $239 and rides on regular bikes lasting up to 45 minutes are included.
Under the new agreement, members could save as much as $8.50 on a single e-bike ride, according to City Hall. The new cap replaces the existing $5.40 cap for rides entering or leaving Manhattan, as well as a one-time allotment of 60 e-bike minutes for members.
The agreement doesn't prohibit Lyft from increasing Citi Bike prices for non-members, who currently pay $4.99 for a ride up to 30 minutes on analog bikes and an additional 41 cents per-minute for e-bike rides.
The city has also agreed to help install electric charging infrastructure at more than 130 Citi Bike stations starting next year. This will allow the e-bikes to recharge while docked, rather than having Lyft workers swap out depleted batteries. City officials said the changes will reduce operating costs and make more e-bikes available to riders.
City Councilmember Lincoln Restler introduced a bill two years ago to rein in the rising cost of Citi Bike rides.
“ This is such a tremendous victory for Citi Bike riders,” Restler said. “The city had given Lyft a monopoly, essentially, with the Citi Bike program and the cost spiraled out of control in such a way where it felt like New Yorkers were being taken advantage of.”
Citi Bike raised prices six times from 2022 through January 2026, with Lyft recently blaming tariffs and inflation for the need to raise rates.
“We’re grateful to Mayor Mamdani and Commissioner Flynn for working with us to make Citi Bike an even more sustainable, reliable, and affordable option for New Yorkers,” Patrick Knoth, general manager of Citi Bike, wrote in a statement.

articles.title_orig: Thanksgiving travel could be messy with storms coming after a week filled with airline glitches
articles.title_zh: Thanksgiving travel could be messy with storms coming after a week filled with airline glitches
articles.content_orig:
Ahead of one of the busiest travel periods of the year, some travelers say they are feeling anxious after last week’s airport chaos.
With less than one week away from Thanksgiving, airports are still facing lingering effects of the nationwide ground stop.
Repeated issues at airports across the country caused a series of delays and cancellations, which leave some flyers to wonder if they’ll get to their loved ones in time for the holiday.
As of Monday morning, there are already seven cancellations and 14 flight delays at Raleigh-Durham International Airport.
“You book these flights way in advance, you pay more for a direct flight, we got our seat assignments with each other and now there’s just like it’s up in the air whether or not we’re going to be able to sit next to each other, or have middle seats; we don’t know,” said Leah Hales, who is traveling through RDU on Monday.
The airport has increased staffing this week to help accommodate passengers.
Remember to plan and give yourself plenty of time to get through the airport. Officials recommend arriving two hours before a domestic flight and three hours before an international one.

articles.title_orig: Oil Futures Extend Decline as Middle East Crude Continues to Flow
articles.title_zh: Oil Futures Extend Decline as Middle East Crude Continues to Flow
articles.content_orig:
Oil prices fell on Monday as traders weighed a rise in supplies from ​the Middle East and the restart of a Libyan oil pipeline, offsetting some unease around shipping and refinery attacks in ‌the region.
Brent crude futures fell $2.58, or 2.8%, to $89.99 a barrel by 1:25 p.m. EDT. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures were down $2.35, or 2.8%, at $81.06 a barrel.
Earlier in the session, Brent hit a session low of $88.60 a barrel, its lowest since August 27, while WTI fell to a low of $79.95, its lowest since August 26.
Libya's Sharara oil pipeline has reopened and crude is beginning to flow into storage tanks at the Akakus facility in Zawiya, ​the chairman of the National Oil Corporation told Reuters on Monday.
Meanwhile, JPMorgan expects oil futures to fall to the ⁠high $70s in the first half of 2027 due to an estimated supply surplus, with higher Middle East production outside Iran next year along ​with more supply from the Americas led by the US.
Bank of America said geopolitics would remain the key driver of oil prices, with relatively low global ​inventories leaving much of the world vulnerable to supply disruptions.
"It is partly the growing signs of a glut, but with each passing day it seems less likely that Trump will attack again," said IG chief market analyst Chris Beauchamp.
On Sunday, however, the Iran-aligned Houthi movement said it attacked a Saudi Arabian oil refinery, while the UK ​Maritime Trade Operations reported multiple attacks on shipping in the Gulf and near the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend.
Bahrain said an Iranian attack hit a civilian ​industrial facility on Saturday, while Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they had launched a missile-and-drone assault on U.S. military positions in the kingdom, home to the U.S. Navy's ‌5th Fleet.
"It ⁠would be irresponsible to conclude that oil will now be supplied uninterruptedly and in vast volumes. Iranian attacks on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz are taking their toll," said PVM analyst Tamas Varga.
Elsewhere, Ukraine's military said on Monday it had struck Russia's Lukoil oil refinery in Perm overnight, damaging three processing units.
The Kaleykino oil pumping station in Tatarstan was also hit, Ukraine's General Staff said on the ​Telegram messaging app, the second strike ​on that site in four days. ⁠Four reservoirs were damaged, it added.
Meanwhile, Russian oil exports from its main oil terminals in the Baltic and Black Sea are facing growing delays due to bad weather and persistent Ukrainian drone attacks, according to traders and people ​with direct knowledge of loading schedules and shipping data.
In Turkey, talks on Sunday at ​the global climate conference ⁠COP31 collapsed for the first time since 2009 after nations could not agree on a deal on including a statement on the phase-out of fossil fuels.
Saudi Arabia and other big oil-producing countries have said fossil fuels will play a role in the economy for the foreseeable future and they lobbied to keep ⁠any mention ​of fossil fuels out of the text, observers at the conference said.
OPEC+ ministers will hold ​a series of meetings on November 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. The group is made up of OPEC and other oil producers such as Russia.
